bib.title: Graph of Thoughts: Solving Elaborate Problems with Large Language Models

read.skipped: Appendix B-E (Tables 3-49, full prompt/response transcripts for sorting, set intersection, keyword counting and NDA merging) skimmed by section map only; the reference list was skimmed.

question: Can modelling LLM reasoning as an arbitrary graph of thoughts, with aggregation and refinement transformations, beat chain, self-consistency and tree prompting on decomposable tasks at lower cost?
hypothesis: Letting thoughts form an arbitrary graph (merging and looping, not just branching) gives stronger prompting than CoT or ToT, especially as problem size grows.
contributions: GoT framework: networked reasoning with thoughts as vertices and dependencies as edges
Modular architecture (Prompter, Parser, Scoring, Controller, GoO, GRS) extensible with new transformations and LLMs
Four use cases: sorting, keyword counting, set operations, document merging
Evaluation showing advantages over the state of the art
Volume of a thought as a metric, and a latency-volume tradeoff analysis

method.summary: A prompting framework in which a user-written Graph of Operations (Generate, Aggregate, Score, KeepBest, Repeat) is executed by a Controller against an LLM, building a graph of thoughts. Compared against IO, CoT, CoT-SC and two ToT variants on four tasks with GPT-3.5, at matched thought counts.
method.task: prompting for decomposable tasks: sorting, set intersection, keyword counting, document merging

datasets.name: Sorting
datasets.size: 100 samples per task and baseline; lists of 32, 64, 128 digits (0-9, duplicates)

datasets.name: Set intersection
datasets.size: 100 samples; sets of 32, 64, 128 elements; 25% to 75% of elements shared

other.note: tried, usually worse than GPT-3.5 and much slower; results not reported

inference.samples: 100 input samples per task and baseline (50 for document merging); number of runs per sample and seeds not stated
inference.prompting: IO, CoT, CoT-SC, ToT (two variants), GoT; few-shot examples in prompts; thought counts fixed per experiment to match cost

parameters.sorting_GoT: split into 16-element chunks; Generate(k=5) sort per chunk (k=3 in Fig 4), KeepBestN(1); Aggregate(10); Generate(k=10) final improve (Listings 5-7)
parameters.set_intersection_GoT: Generate(k=5) per 16-element subset, Aggregate(10) (5 for 128 elements) (Listings 1-4)
parameters.ToT: two variants, higher k / lower depth L (ToT) and lower k / higher L (ToT2); e.g. sorting L=2 k=20 vs L=3 k=10 for 32 elements, L=4 k=20 vs L=7 k=10 for 64, L=4 k=20 vs L=10 k=10 for 128 (read from Fig 5)
parameters.keyword_counting_GoT: GoT4 (4 passages, aggregate 2 at a time), GoT8 (8 passages), GoTx (sentence split with shrunk few-shot examples)
parameters.document_merging_scoring: LLM queried for redundancy and retention, 3 times each, averaged; harmonic mean

other.cost: example given: 80 vs 60 total responses cost $6 vs $3 (Fig 7)

metrics.name: error-scope (sorting)
metrics.definition: X + Y; X counts adjacent out-of-order pairs, Y sums over digits 0-9 the absolute difference between input and output counts; clipped at n in plots

metrics.name: error-scope (set intersection)
metrics.definition: X1 + X2 + Xd: extra elements, missing elements, duplicates

metrics.name: keyword counting error
metrics.definition: sum over keywords of absolute difference between computed and correct count

metrics.name: document merging score
metrics.definition: harmonic mean of redundancy and information retention, each 0-10

metrics.name: total cost
metrics.definition: cost of API calls for the experiment

metrics.name: volume of a thought
metrics.definition: number of thoughts from which a directed path reaches it

eval.protocol: 100 samples per task and baseline, distributions shown as quartiles/medians in figures; thought counts fixed to match cost; no significance test stated

prompts.purpose: Sort a 16-number chunk (Generate k=1 + Repeat k=4)
prompts.text:
<Instruction> Sort the following list of numbers in ascending order. Output only the sorted list of numbers, no additional text. </Instruction>
<Example> ... </Example>
Input: {input}

prompts.purpose: Merge two sorted lists (Aggregate + Repeat k=3 + KeepBest N=1)
prompts.text: <Instruction> Merge the following 2 sorted lists of length {length1} each, into one sorted list of length {length2} using a merge sort style approach. Only output the final merged list without any additional text or thoughts! </Instruction>

limits: Only GPT-3.5 evaluated in the reported results; Llama-2 was worse and too slow, results not shown (budget restrictions).
CoT-SC results omitted from the figures as not informative.
The Graph of Operations is hand-designed per task and static, built before execution; the Controller just follows the plan.
Tasks chosen are naturally decomposable (sorting, set ops, counting, merging); the authors say GoT suits such tasks, no evidence for others.
Exact numbers mostly appear only in figures; no significance tests; seeds and API settings other than temperature not given.
